key_terms.meaning: Partial pressure of a component in an ideal liquid mixture: pᵢ = xᵢ·Pᵢˢᵃᵗ, where xᵢ is liquid mole fraction and Pᵢˢᵃᵗ its pure-component vapour pressure at that temperature.
α = (y<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>A</sub>)/(y<sub>B</sub>/x<sub>B</sub>) = P<sub>A</sub>ˢᵃᵗ/P<sub>B</sub>ˢᵃᵗ for an ideal pair; α > 1 means A is the more volatile component.
One equilibrium stage in which a pressurised feed is heated and throttled so it partly vaporises; vapour and liquid leave in equilibrium.
Moles of vapour formed per mole of feed in a flash; fixed by feed enthalpy and equilibrium, not chosen freely.
ln(L₁/L₂) = ∫(dx/(y − x)) from x₂ to x₁, the material balance for simple distillation with no reflux.
Boiling an immiscible organic liquid with steam so the total pressure is p<sub>organic</sub> + p<sub>water</sub>, lowering the boiling temperature.
Material-balance line on the y-x diagram, y = (R/(R+1))x + x<sub>D</sub>/(R+1) for the rectifying section.
Line through the feed point with slope q/(q−1); q is the moles of liquid added to the stripping section per mole of feed.
Alternating horizontal steps to the equilibrium curve and vertical steps to the operating line; each pair of steps is one theoretical stage.
R = L/D, the moles of liquid returned to the column per mole of distillate withdrawn.
R<sub>min</sub>, the reflux at which the operating line touches the equilibrium curve (the pinch), so the stage count becomes infinite.
Point where the operating line meets the equilibrium curve, so no further change in composition is possible.
Enthalpy-balance point Δ in the Ponchon-Savarit method from which operating lines are drawn, replacing the constant-molar-overflow assumption.
Plot of specific enthalpy against mole fraction, with saturated liquid and saturated vapour lines and tie lines joining equilibrium phases.
E<sub>M</sub> = (y<sub>n</sub> − y<sub>n+1</sub>)/(y<sub>n</sub>* − y<sub>n+1</sub>): the vapour enrichment a real tray gives divided by the enrichment an equilibrium tray would give.
Height equivalent to a theoretical plate; packed height needed = HETP × number of theoretical stages.
N<sub>min</sub> = log[(d/b)<sub>LK</sub> (b/d)<sub>HK</sub>]/log α<sub>LK-HK</sub>, the minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux for the key split.
Empirical plot of (N − N<sub>min</sub>)/(N + 1) against (R − R<sub>min</sub>)/(R + 1) that gives the actual stage count at a chosen R.
A mixture whose liquid and vapour compositions are equal at the boiling point, so it distils with no change in composition.
A heavy, high-boiling solvent fed near the top changes the relative volatility and removes the azeotrope barrier.
Σ α<sub>i</sub> z<sub>i</sub>/(α<sub>i</sub> − θ) = 1 − q gives θ between the key volatilities; R<sub>min</sub> + 1 = Σ α<sub>i</sub> x<sub>D,i</sub>/(α<sub>i</sub> − θ).
Boiling an organic with immiscible water: P = p°<sub>water</sub> + p°<sub>organic</sub>, so it boils below 100 °C at 1 atm; mol steam per mol organic = p°<sub>water</sub>/p°<sub>organic</sub>.

takeaways: Vapour and liquid compositions in equilibrium are fixed by component vapour pressures and total pressure; for an ideal pair the single number α tells you how easy the separation is.
A flash gives only one equilibrium stage, so it can only make a rough split; the vapour fraction is set by the feed enthalpy.
Simple distillation is batch without reflux and its performance is given by the Rayleigh equation; steam distillation lowers the boiling temperature by sharing the total pressure.
The McCabe-Thiele method replaces the column by stepping between the equilibrium curve and the operating lines, with the q-line fixing where the feed enters.
Lower reflux means fewer stages but the stage count explodes as R falls to R<sub>min</sub>; total reflux gives N<sub>min</sub>.
Ponchon-Savarit does not assume constant molar overflow, so it stays valid for unequal latent heats and concentrated solutions.
Real trays give less separation than an ideal stage, so the theoretical stages are divided by the tray efficiency to get actual trays; packing is rated by HETP.
For multicomponent mixtures use shortcuts: Fenske for minimum stages, Underwood for minimum reflux, Gilliland to get stages at the chosen reflux.
An azeotrope cannot be crossed by ordinary distillation; a separating agent (pressure change, azeotropic entrainer or solvent) shifts the equilibrium.
bank_note: Long answers almost always ask for a labelled y-x or enthalpy-composition construction with a worked number of stages, so keep the construction, the assumptions (constant molar overflow, constant α) and the numeric answer in view; shortcut methods and azeotropes come as separate questions.

bank.q: State Raoult's law and Dalton's law and derive the equilibrium relation y = αx / (1 + (α − 1)x) for a binary ideal mixture.
outline: Raoult: p<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>, p<sub>B</sub> = x<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>
Dalton: P = p<sub>A</sub> + p<sub>B</sub>, y<sub>A</sub> = p<sub>A</sub>/P, y<sub>B</sub> = p<sub>B</sub>/P
Divide y<sub>A</sub>/y<sub>B</sub> = (x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>)/(x<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>), so α = P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>
Put y<sub>B</sub> = 1 − y<sub>A</sub> and x<sub>B</sub> = 1 − x<sub>A</sub> and solve for y<sub>A</sub>
Note α depends on temperature, so use an average α over the column
answer: Raoult's law. For an ideal liquid mixture the partial pressure of each component above the liquid equals its liquid mole fraction times its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature: p<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> and p<sub>B</sub> = x<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>. It holds when A and B are chemically similar (benzene-toluene, hexane-heptane), so that A-B attractions equal the A-A and B-B ones; the activity coefficients are then 1.

Dalton's law. In an ideal gas mixture each component exerts its partial pressure independently, and the total pressure is their sum: P = p<sub>A</sub> + p<sub>B</sub>. The vapour mole fraction of A is its share of the total: y<sub>A</sub> = p<sub>A</sub>/P, and similarly y<sub>B</sub> = p<sub>B</sub>/P.

Combining the two. y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P and y<sub>B</sub> = x<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P. Adding the partial pressures gives the bubble-point condition P = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> + (1 − x<sub>A</sub>)P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>, so x<sub>A</sub> = (P − P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>)/(P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> − P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>).

Relative volatility. Define α = (y<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>A</sub>)/(y<sub>B</sub>/x<sub>B</sub>). Substituting the two expressions for y, the P cancels: α = (P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P)/(P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P) = P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>/P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>. For an ideal pair α is simply the ratio of the pure vapour pressures; A is the more volatile component when α > 1.

Deriving the y-x relation. From the definition, y<sub>A</sub>/(1 − y<sub>A</sub>) = α x<sub>A</sub>/(1 − x<sub>A</sub>), since y<sub>B</sub> = 1 − y<sub>A</sub> and x<sub>B</sub> = 1 − x<sub>A</sub>. Cross-multiply: y<sub>A</sub>(1 − x<sub>A</sub>) = α x<sub>A</sub>(1 − y<sub>A</sub>). Expand: y<sub>A</sub> − y<sub>A</sub> x<sub>A</sub> = α x<sub>A</sub> − α x<sub>A</sub> y<sub>A</sub>. Collect the y<sub>A</sub> terms: y<sub>A</sub>(1 − x<sub>A</sub> + α x<sub>A</sub>) = α x<sub>A</sub>. Hence y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x], dropping the subscript A.

answer: Assumptions and limits. Both laws assume ideal behaviour: an ideal liquid (no heat of mixing, no volume change) and an ideal vapour (moderate pressure). P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> and P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup> both rise with temperature but not in the same proportion, so α changes along a column, which runs hotter at the bottom. Designers use a mean, often the geometric mean of the top and bottom values, α<sub>avg</sub> = √(α<sub>top</sub> α<sub>bottom</sub>).

Non-ideal mixtures. When the liquid is not ideal, Raoult's law becomes p<sub>A</sub> = γ<sub>A</sub> x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> with an activity coefficient γ<sub>A</sub>. Then α = γ<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup>/(γ<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup>) varies strongly with composition and can reach 1 at an azeotrope, where the y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x] curve with a constant α no longer describes the data.

Use. The relation y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x] is the equilibrium curve drawn on every McCabe-Thiele diagram, and its inverse x = y/[α − (α − 1)y] is used when stepping stages. Closing check: at x = 0.5 and α = 3, y = 1.5/2 = 0.75, which lies above the diagonal as it must for α > 1.

bank.q: Explain flash distillation with a neat sketch of the equipment and state what decides the fraction vaporised.
outline: Feed heated in a furnace, throttled through a valve into a low-pressure drum
Vapour and liquid separate in the drum and leave in equilibrium
Mass balance F = V + L and component balance Fz = Vy + Lx
Equilibrium relation y = f(x) links the compositions
Enthalpy balance fixes V/F; degree of freedom argument shows V/F is not free
answer: Principle. Flash (equilibrium) distillation partly vaporises a liquid feed in a single step and lets the vapour and liquid separate while they are in equilibrium. It gives one theoretical stage, so the separation is coarse, but it needs no column, no trays and no reflux.

answer.text: Equipment, as in the sketch. The pressurised feed is heated in a heater or furnace to a temperature above its bubble point at the drum pressure, but it stays liquid because its pressure is high. It is throttled through a valve into a drum at lower pressure; part of it flashes to vapour. The vapour rises through a mist eliminator and leaves at the top; the liquid collects and leaves at the bottom.

answer: Material balances. Overall: F = V + L. Component: Fz = Vy + Lx, where F, V and L are molar flows and z, y and x the mole fractions of the more volatile component. Dividing by F with f = V/F: z = f y + (1 − f) x, which rearranges to the operating line y = −[(1 − f)/f]x + z/f. It passes through (z, z) on the diagonal with slope −L/V.

Equilibrium. The products leave in equilibrium, y = K x, or for a binary of constant α, y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x]. The answer is the intersection of the operating line with the equilibrium curve. For many components each one obeys y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>, and combining Σx<sub>i</sub> = 1 with Σy<sub>i</sub> = 1 gives the Rachford-Rice equation Σ z<sub>i</sub>(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)/[1 + f(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 0.

What decides the fraction vaporised. The vapour fraction f is not a free choice once the drum conditions are set. In an isothermal flash, fixing the drum temperature and pressure fixes every K<sub>i</sub>, and Rachford-Rice then gives one f. In an adiabatic flash the feed enthalpy and drum pressure are fixed; the enthalpy balance F h<sub>F</sub> = V H<sub>V</sub> + L h<sub>L</sub>, solved together with equilibrium, gives both the drum temperature and f. Raising the feed temperature or lowering the drum pressure raises f; raising the pressure lowers every K and so lowers f.

Degrees of freedom. For a binary feed of known F, z and enthalpy, specifying the drum pressure leaves one more specification: temperature, f, or one product composition. Choose one and the others follow; specifying two of them over-fixes the problem.

Uses. Pre-flash ahead of crude distillation, removing light gases from a liquid product, flashing hot condensate, and multi-stage flash desalination. Closing check: 50(0.667) + 50(0.333) = 50.0 = 100(0.50), so the component balance closes.

bank.q: Explain steam distillation. Why does adding steam reduce the boiling temperature of an organic liquid?
outline: Organic and water are immiscible, so each exerts its own vapour pressure
Total pressure = p<sub>organic</sub> + p<sub>water</sub>
Boiling starts when the sum equals the applied pressure
Each component boils below its own normal boiling point
Steam needed: moles of steam per mole of organic = p<sub>water</sub>/p<sub>organic</sub>
Used for heat-sensitive, high-boiling organics
answer: Purpose. Many high-boiling organics (essential oils, aniline, fatty acids) decompose at their normal boiling points. Steam distillation lets them distil well below that temperature, at atmospheric pressure, without a vacuum system.

Immiscible liquids. Water and the organic are practically insoluble in each other, so they form two separate liquid layers. Each layer behaves as a pure liquid and exerts its full pure-component vapour pressure, whatever the amount of the other: p<sub>water</sub> = p°<sub>water</sub>(T) and p<sub>organic</sub> = p°<sub>organic</sub>(T). Raoult's law with mole fractions does not apply because there is no common solution.

Boiling condition. The mixture boils when the sum of the two vapour pressures equals the applied pressure: P = p°<sub>water</sub>(T) + p°<sub>organic</sub>(T). Because the two pressures add, the sum reaches P at a temperature where each pressure is below P. So the mixture boils below 100 °C (the water alone) and well below the organic's own boiling point.

Steam requirement. In the vapour the mole ratio of the two components equals the ratio of their partial pressures. Moles of steam per mole of organic = p°<sub>water</sub>/p°<sub>organic</sub>. The mass of steam per kg of organic = (p°<sub>water</sub>/p°<sub>organic</sub>)(18/M<sub>organic</sub>). A high molar mass therefore keeps the mass of steam small even when the molar ratio is large.

answer: Equipment. Live steam is sparged through the organic charge in a still. The mixed vapour is condensed, and the condensate separates in a decanter (a Florentine flask for essential oils) into an organic layer and a water layer.

Practical points. Real steam use is higher than the ideal ratio because the steam is not fully saturated with organic and some condenses to heat the charge; superheated steam reduces the condensation. The organic must be immiscible with water and must not react with it.

bank.q: Define reflux ratio, minimum reflux ratio and total reflux, and explain their effect on the McCabe-Thiele construction.
outline: R = L/D
Higher R: operating line further from equilibrium, fewer stages, more liquid and vapour traffic
R<sub>min</sub>: operating line touches equilibrium at the pinch, infinite stages
Total reflux: R → ∞, operating line is the diagonal y = x, minimum stages
Sketch the three constructions
answer: Reflux ratio. R = L/D, the liquid returned to the top of the column per mole of distillate. The vapour to the condenser is V = (R + 1)D. On the y-x diagram the rectifying operating line is y = [R/(R + 1)]x + x<sub>D</sub>/(R + 1), through (x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>D</sub>) with slope R/(R + 1).

Effect of R. Raising R steepens the rectifying line toward the diagonal and moves it away from the equilibrium curve. The steps between curve and line then grow and fewer stages reach x<sub>B</sub>. The cost is more liquid and vapour traffic, so a wider column and larger reboiler and condenser duties, which grow as (R + 1)D.

Minimum reflux. As R falls the operating line approaches the equilibrium curve. At R<sub>min</sub> the two touch at the pinch; there the driving force is zero and the staircase never passes the pinch, so the stage count is infinite. For a saturated-liquid feed and an ideal curve the pinch lies on the q-line at x<sub>F</sub>: R<sub>min</sub> = (x<sub>D</sub> − y<sub>F</sub>*)/(y<sub>F</sub>* − x<sub>F</sub>). For a non-ideal curve a tangent pinch above the feed may come first.

Total reflux. No product is drawn: R → ∞, the operating lines lie on the diagonal y = x, and the steps between curve and diagonal give the minimum number of stages, N<sub>min</sub>. For constant α, Fenske gives N<sub>min</sub> = log[(x<sub>D</sub>/(1 − x<sub>D</sub>))((1 − x<sub>B</sub>)/x<sub>B</sub>)]/log α. It is used at start-up and for efficiency tests.

answer: Sketches. (a) Design R: two operating lines meeting on the q-line, a finite staircase. (b) Minimum reflux: the rectifying line from (x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>D</sub>) passes through (x<sub>F</sub>, y<sub>F</sub>*) on the curve, and the steps crowd into the pinch. (c) Total reflux: both lines on the diagonal, the fewest and largest steps.
Closing check: the design R = 2.0 lies between R<sub>min</sub> = 1.44 and ∞, and its 13 stages lie between N<sub>min</sub> = 6.4 and infinity, as they must.

bank.q: A binary feed of 100 kmol/h with 40 mol% of the more volatile component is flashed at 1 atm. Given α = 2.5 and the equilibrium relation y = 2.5x/(1+1.5x), calculate the vapour and liquid flows and compositions when V/F = 0.3.
outline: Material balances: F = V + L, Fz = Vy + Lx
Substitute V = 0.3F, L = 0.7F and z = 0.40
Combine with the equilibrium relation to get one equation in x
Solve the quadratic, then get y
Report V, L in kmol/h and x, y as mole fractions
answer: Data. F = 100 kmol/h, z = 0.40, V/F = f = 0.3, α = 2.5, so V = 0.3 × 100 = 30 kmol/h and L = 70 kmol/h. Equilibrium: y = 2.5x/(1 + 1.5x).

Material balances. F = V + L and Fz = Vy + Lx. Divided by F: 0.40 = 0.3y + 0.7x. As an operating line: y = −(0.7/0.3)x + 0.40/0.3 = −2.333x + 1.333, passing through (0.40, 0.40) with slope −L/V = −2.333.
One equation in x. Substitute the equilibrium relation: 0.40 = 0.3[2.5x/(1 + 1.5x)] + 0.7x. Multiply through by (1 + 1.5x): 0.40(1 + 1.5x) = 0.75x + 0.7x(1 + 1.5x).
K values at the drum: K<sub>A</sub> = 0.556/0.333 = 1.667 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.444/0.667 = 0.667, ratio 2.5 = α, consistent with the equilibrium relation.

Graphical method. On the y-x diagram, draw the equilibrium curve y = 2.5x/(1 + 1.5x) and the diagonal, mark (0.40, 0.40) and draw the line of slope −2.333 through it. It cuts the curve at (0.333, 0.556), the same answer, which is the quick exam check.

Rachford-Rice route. The same answer follows from Σ z<sub>i</sub>(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)/[1 + f(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 0 with K<sub>A</sub> = 1.667 and K<sub>B</sub> = 0.667 found at the drum: 0.40(0.667)/[1 + 0.3(0.667)] + 0.60(−0.333)/[1 + 0.3(−0.333)] = 0.2222 − 0.2222 = 0. In an exam the K values are usually not given for a binary of constant α, so the quadratic route is the direct one.

Effect of f. Repeating the calculation for other vapour fractions shows the trade-off of a single stage: at f = 0.5 the quadratic 0.75x² + 1.15x − 0.40 = 0 gives x = 0.292 and y = 0.508, against 0.333 and 0.556 at f = 0.3: a bigger cut takes more of A overhead (25.4 against 16.7 kmol/h) but at lower purity.

Interpretation. The vapour is enriched from 0.40 to 0.556 and the liquid depleted to 0.333: a single stage gives only a modest split, which is why columns repeat the contact. Raising f would make both products leaner in A: at f → 1 the vapour approaches the feed composition.
Answer: V = 30 kmol/h with y = 0.556; L = 70 kmol/h with x = 0.333. Closing check: 30(0.556) + 70(0.333) = 16.7 + 23.3 = 40.0 kmol/h of A, equal to the feed.

bank.q: Using the Rayleigh equation, find the amount of distillate and its average composition when a batch of 100 kmol of a 0.5 mole fraction mixture is distilled until the residue reaches 0.2 mole fraction. Relative volatility is 2.2.
outline: Write ln(L₁/L₂) = ∫ dx/(y − x)
Insert y from the α relation and integrate analytically
Substitute x₁ = 0.5, x₂ = 0.2 to get L₂
Distillate D = L₁ − L₂
Average composition from the component balance x<sub>D,avg</sub> = (L₁x₁ − L₂x₂)/D
answer: Data. L<sub>1</sub> = 100 kmol at x<sub>1</sub> = 0.5; distil until x<sub>2</sub> = 0.2; constant α = 2.2. Simple (differential) distillation: no reflux, the vapour removed at each instant is in equilibrium with the pot liquid.

Rayleigh equation. A balance on the more volatile component as dL moles boil off gives d(Lx) = y dL, so L dx = (y − x) dL and ln(L<sub>1</sub>/L<sub>2</sub>) = ∫ from x<sub>2</sub> to x<sub>1</sub> of dx/(y − x).

Constant α. Put y = αx/[1 + (α − 1)x]. Then y − x = (α − 1)x(1 − x)/[1 + (α − 1)x], and by partial fractions the integral becomes ln(L<sub>1</sub>/L<sub>2</sub>) = [ln(x<sub>1</sub>/x<sub>2</sub>) + α ln((1 − x<sub>2</sub>)/(1 − x<sub>1</sub>))]/(α − 1), the same as [ln(x<sub>1</sub>/x<sub>2</sub>) − α ln((1 − x<sub>1</sub>)/(1 − x<sub>2</sub>))]/(α − 1).
Residue: L<sub>2</sub> = 100/5.080 = 19.7 kmol. Distillate: D = L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub> = 100 − 19.7 = 80.3 kmol.

Average distillate composition from the component balance: x<sub>D,avg</sub> = (L<sub>1</sub> x<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub> x<sub>2</sub>)/D = (100 × 0.5 − 19.69 × 0.2)/80.31 = (50 − 3.94)/80.31 = 0.574.

Instantaneous compositions. At the start the vapour is y = 2.2(0.5)/(1 + 1.2 × 0.5) = 0.688; at the end y = 2.2(0.2)/(1 + 1.2 × 0.2) = 0.355. The collected distillate averages 0.574, between the two, as it must.

Comparison with α = 2.0. The chapter example with α = 2.0 left 15.6 kmol with x<sub>D,avg</sub> = 0.556. The larger α here strips the light component faster, so the pot reaches 0.2 with more liquid left (19.7 kmol) and a richer distillate (0.574).
Graphical integration. If α were not constant, plot 1/(y − x) against x from the VLE data between 0.2 and 0.5 and measure the area; the area equals ln(L<sub>1</sub>/L<sub>2</sub>).

Assumptions. The pot liquid is perfectly mixed, the vapour leaving at each instant is in equilibrium with it (one theoretical stage), there is no entrainment and no reflux, and α stays at 2.2 over the range. In practice the still head gives a little enrichment, so a real still does slightly better than this calculation.

Stopping point. If the distillate had to average at least 0.60, the run would have to stop earlier, at a higher x<sub>2</sub>: the average composition falls as more of the charge is boiled away, so purity and recovery trade against each other.

Answer: distillate 80.3 kmol of average composition 0.574; residue 19.7 kmol at 0.2. Closing check on the more volatile component: 80.31 × 0.5735 + 19.69 × 0.2 = 46.06 + 3.94 = 50.0 kmol, equal to the charge.

bank.q: A column separates a feed of 45 mol% A into a distillate of 95 mol% A and a bottoms of 5 mol% A. The relative volatility is 2.5, the feed is saturated liquid and R = 2.0. Determine the number of theoretical stages by McCabe-Thiele and locate the feed stage.
outline: Plot the equilibrium curve and the diagonal
Rectifying operating line: intercept x<sub>D</sub>/(R+1), passes through (x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>D</sub>)
q-line for saturated liquid is vertical at x = z<sub>F</sub>
Stripping line through (x<sub>B</sub>, x<sub>B</sub>) and the q-line intersection
Step off stages, count including a partial reboiler, mark the change of operating line as the feed stage
Report stages as a number, not a fraction
answer: Data and assumptions. x<sub>F</sub> = 0.45 saturated liquid (q = 1), x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, x<sub>B</sub> = 0.05, R = 2.0, α = 2.5 (equilibrium y = 2.5x/(1 + 1.5x)), total condenser, partial reboiler, constant molar overflow.

Product split on 100 kmol/h of feed: D = F(x<sub>F</sub> − x<sub>B</sub>)/(x<sub>D</sub> − x<sub>B</sub>) = 100(0.40)/0.90 = 44.4 kmol/h; B = 55.6 kmol/h. Rectifying flows: L = RD = 88.9, V = (R + 1)D = 133.3 kmol/h. Stripping flows with q = 1: L′ = L + F = 188.9, V′ = V = 133.3 kmol/h.
Rectifying operating line: y = [R/(R + 1)]x + x<sub>D</sub>/(R + 1) = 0.6667x + 0.3167, from (0.95, 0.95).

q-line: saturated liquid, so it is the vertical line x = 0.45. It meets the rectifying line at y = 0.6667(0.45) + 0.3167 = 0.6167: P = (0.45, 0.6167). Check: the equilibrium y at 0.45 is 2.5(0.45)/1.675 = 0.672, above P, so the column can work.
Stepping rule. Start at (0.95, 0.95). Horizontal to the equilibrium curve gives x = y/(2.5 − 1.5y); vertical to the rectifying line while x > 0.45, then to the stripping line. Stop when x ≤ 0.05.

Why the lines are straight. Constant molar overflow assumes equal molar latent heats, no heat of mixing and an adiabatic column, so each mole of vapour condensed boils one mole of liquid and L, V (and L′, V′) do not change within a section. Each operating line is then a straight material-balance line, and the q-line, y = [q/(q − 1)]x − x<sub>F</sub>/(q − 1), becomes vertical when q = 1.

svg.aria: McCabe-Thiele diagram with equilibrium curve for alpha 2.5, operating lines meeting on a vertical q-line at x 0.45, and a 12-step staircase with the feed on step 6.

answer: Feed stage. Stage 5 leaves x = 0.4858, still above 0.45; stage 6 leaves x = 0.4162, below it, so stage 6 straddles the q-line and is the optimum feed stage. Switching there gives the fewest stages.

Stage count. The 12th step passes x<sub>B</sub> (0.0243 < 0.05). The last step is the partial reboiler, so the column has 12 theoretical stages: 11 ideal trays plus the reboiler, with the feed on the 6th stage from the top. Only about a fifth of the last step is used ((0.0561 − 0.05)/(0.0561 − 0.0243) = 0.19), so the exact count is about 11.2, rounded up to 12.

Reading the diagram. Each horizontal move from the operating line to the equilibrium curve is one equilibrium contact: the vapour y leaving a stage and the liquid x leaving the same stage are in equilibrium. Each vertical move from the curve to the operating line uses the material balance to find the vapour rising from the stage below. Stepping from the top keeps the rectifying line until the step passes the q-line, which is why the feed stage is the step that straddles it.

Effect of the feed condition. Had the feed entered as saturated vapour (q = 0) at the same composition, the q-line would be horizontal at y = 0.45, the operating lines would meet lower, the stripping section would need more stages and R<sub>min</sub> would rise; a cold liquid feed (q > 1) does the opposite. This is why the feed condition must be stated with the stage count.

Actual trays. With an overall tray efficiency of, say, 0.65, the 11 ideal trays become 11/0.65 = 16.9, so 17 actual trays, and the feed tray moves to about the 6/0.65 ≈ 9th tray from the top. The partial reboiler is not divided by the efficiency because it is already an equilibrium stage.
Margin from minimum reflux. y<sub>F</sub>* = 0.672, so R<sub>min</sub> = (0.95 − 0.672)/(0.672 − 0.45) = 1.256; the design R = 2.0 is 1.59 R<sub>min</sub>, in the usual range.
Comparison. With x<sub>F</sub> = 0.40 the same column needed 13 stages; the richer feed here leaves less work for the rectifying section and moves the feed stage up from 7 to 6.

Answer: 12 theoretical stages including the reboiler (11 ideal trays), feed on stage 6 from the top. Closing check: the overall balance 44.4(0.95) + 55.6(0.05) = 42.2 + 2.8 = 45.0 kmol/h of A equals the feed.

bank.q: For a ternary feed, explain how you would find the minimum number of stages, the minimum reflux, and the number of stages at R = 1.5 R<sub>min</sub> using shortcut methods. Give the working equations.
outline: Choose light and heavy keys, distribute the non-key components
Fenske: N<sub>min</sub> = log[(d/b)<sub>LK</sub> (b/d)<sub>HK</sub>]/log α<sub>avg</sub>
Underwood θ from Σ αᵢzᵢf/(αᵢ − θ) = 1 − q, then R<sub>min</sub> = Σ αᵢx<sub>D</sub>ᵢ/(αᵢ − θ) − 1
Gilliland correlation between (N − N<sub>min</sub>)/(N+1) and (R − R<sub>min</sub>)/(R+1)
State that these are shortcuts and need rigorous stage-wise checking
answer: Approach. Rigorous multicomponent design solves the stage equations by computer. The shortcut (Fenske-Underwood-Gilliland) gives the minimum stages, the minimum reflux and the stage count at a chosen reflux from a few equations, assuming constant relative volatility and constant molar overflow.

Step 1, keys. Choose the light key (LK), the more volatile component whose recovery in the distillate is specified, and the heavy key (HK), the less volatile one whose recovery in the bottoms is specified. Components lighter than the LK go almost wholly to the distillate; those heavier than the HK go to the bottoms. Express α<sub>i</sub> relative to the HK.

Step 2, Fenske (total reflux): N<sub>min</sub> = log[(d/b)<sub>LK</sub> (b/d)<sub>HK</sub>]/log α<sub>LK-HK</sub>, with d and b the component flows in distillate and bottoms. With N<sub>min</sub> known, the non-key split follows from (d/b)<sub>i</sub> = (d/b)<sub>HK</sub> α<sub>i</sub><sup>N<sub>min</sub></sup>.

Step 3, Underwood (minimum reflux). Solve Σ α<sub>i</sub> z<sub>i</sub>/(α<sub>i</sub> − θ) = 1 − q for the root θ between α<sub>HK</sub> and α<sub>LK</sub>, then R<sub>min</sub> + 1 = Σ α<sub>i</sub> x<sub>D,i</sub>/(α<sub>i</sub> − θ) over all components in the distillate.

Step 4, Gilliland. With R = 1.5 R<sub>min</sub> form X = (R − R<sub>min</sub>)/(R + 1), read Y = (N − N<sub>min</sub>)/(N + 1) from the chart or the Molokanov fit Y = 1 − exp{[(1 + 54.4X)/(11 + 117.2X)][(X − 1)/√X]}, and solve N = (N<sub>min</sub> + Y)/(1 − Y).

answer.text: Worked case: 100 kmol/h saturated liquid, benzene 0.40 (α = 2.5, LK), toluene 0.35 (α = 1.0, HK), o-xylene 0.25 (α = 0.45); 98 % recovery of each key.

answer: Feed location. The Kirkbride equation, log(N<sub>R</sub>/N<sub>S</sub>) = 0.206 log[(B/D)(z<sub>HK</sub>/z<sub>LK</sub>)(x<sub>B,LK</sub>/x<sub>D,HK</sub>)²], places the feed; here it gives N<sub>R</sub>/N<sub>S</sub> = 0.94, so the feed enters close to the middle of the column.

Limits. The shortcut assumes constant α and CMO; a wide-boiling feed, a non-ideal mixture or a distributing non-key needs a rigorous stage-to-stage check. Underwood θ must be the root between the key volatilities, and every component's own α<sub>i</sub> must appear in both sums.

Answer for the worked case: N<sub>min</sub> = 8.5, R<sub>min</sub> = 1.25, and at R = 1.5 R<sub>min</sub> = 1.875 about 17 theoretical stages including the reboiler. Closing check: 17 lies between N<sub>min</sub> = 8.5 and the 19 stages the same feed needs at the lower reflux 1.3 R<sub>min</sub>.

bank.q: A McCabe-Thiele construction gives 12 theoretical stages. The column uses sieve trays with an overall efficiency of 60%. Find the number of actual trays and explain the meaning of the efficiency value.
outline: Actual trays = theoretical stages / efficiency
12/0.60 = 20 actual trays
Efficiency less than 1 because contact time is finite and trays are not perfectly mixed
If the 12 stages include a partial reboiler, trays = 11/0.60 = 18.3 → 19; state which basis is used
answer: Overall efficiency. E<sub>o</sub> = N<sub>t</sub>/N<sub>a</sub>, the theoretical stages divided by the actual trays needed for the same separation. Rearranged, N<sub>a</sub> = N<sub>t</sub>/E<sub>o</sub>.
Calculation. If the 12 theoretical stages are all column trays (a total reboiler that does no separation, or a stage count quoted for the column alone): N<sub>a</sub> = 12/0.60 = 20 actual trays.

Reboiler basis. A partial reboiler is itself an equilibrium stage and is counted in a McCabe-Thiele staircase. If the 12 stages include it, only 11 are trays: N<sub>a</sub> = 11/0.60 = 18.3, rounded up to 19 actual trays plus the reboiler. A partial condenser, when present, is also an equilibrium stage and is removed the same way. State the basis in the answer.
Rounding. Always round up: 18.3 trays cannot be built and 18 would fall short of the separation.

Meaning of 60 %. On a real sieve tray the vapour and liquid are in contact for a fraction of a second, the liquid is not perfectly mixed across the tray, and some liquid is carried up as entrainment or weeps down through the holes. The vapour therefore leaves less enriched than an equilibrium stage would make it. An overall efficiency of 0.60 means the column needs 1/0.60 = 1.67 real trays for each ideal stage.

Murphree efficiency. The local measure is E<sub>M</sub> = (y<sub>n</sub> − y<sub>n+1</sub>)/(y<sub>n</sub>* − y<sub>n+1</sub>), the real enrichment of the vapour across tray n divided by the enrichment an equilibrium tray would give. With straight lines, Lewis's relation E<sub>o</sub> = ln[1 + E<sub>M</sub>(λ − 1)]/ln λ links the two, λ = mV/L.

What sets the value. Typical E<sub>o</sub> for hydrocarbon sieve trays is 0.6 to 0.8; viscous liquids, high relative volatility and poor hydraulics lower it. O'Connell's correlation estimates E<sub>o</sub> from the product of α and the liquid viscosity.
Answer: 20 actual trays if the 12 stages are trays only; 19 trays plus the reboiler if one of the 12 is the partial reboiler. Closing check: 19 × 0.60 = 11.4 ≥ 11 ideal trays, and 20 × 0.60 = 12.

bank.q: Explain the Ponchon-Savarit construction on an enthalpy-concentration diagram and show how the difference points are located for a given feed.
outline: Plot saturated liquid and saturated vapour lines and tie lines
Locate Δ<sub>D</sub> at (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>) with H<sub>ΔD</sub> = h<sub>D</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub>/D = H<sub>1</sub> + R(H<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>D</sub>)
Locate Δ<sub>B</sub> below x<sub>B</sub>
Feed point F on the h-z line; Δ<sub>D</sub>, F, Δ<sub>B</sub> are collinear
Operating lines are drawn from Δ points through points on the saturated lines
Count stages by alternating tie lines and operating lines
answer: Purpose. Ponchon-Savarit designs a binary column without constant molar overflow by carrying the enthalpy balance on an enthalpy-composition diagram. It is needed when latent heats differ, heats of mixing are large or the boiling range is wide.

The diagram. Plot the saturated-vapour enthalpy H against y and the saturated-liquid enthalpy h against x, both per mole of mixture, on the same axes. Equilibrium tie lines join each liquid x to its vapour y. The vertical gap H − h is the latent heat.

Rectifying difference point. Around the condenser: V<sub>1</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + D, and the enthalpy balance V<sub>1</sub> H<sub>1</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> h<sub>D</sub> + D h<sub>D</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub>. Define H<sub>ΔD</sub> = h<sub>D</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub>/D. With R = L<sub>0</sub>/D this becomes H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>1</sub> + R(H<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>D</sub>). Δ<sub>D</sub> = (x<sub>D</sub>, H<sub>ΔD</sub>) lies above the H curve.

Why the lines are straight. For any section above the feed, V<sub>n+1</sub> − L<sub>n</sub> = D, V<sub>n+1</sub>y<sub>n+1</sub> − L<sub>n</sub> x<sub>n</sub> = Dx<sub>D</sub> and V<sub>n+1</sub>H<sub>n+1</sub> − L<sub>n</sub> h<sub>n</sub> = D H<sub>ΔD</sub>. So (x<sub>n</sub>, h<sub>n</sub>), (y<sub>n+1</sub>, H<sub>n+1</sub>) and Δ<sub>D</sub> lie on one straight line: the operating line. The lever rule on it gives L<sub>n</sub>/V<sub>n+1</sub> = (H<sub>ΔD</sub> − H<sub>n+1</sub>)/(H<sub>ΔD</sub> − h<sub>n</sub>).

Stripping difference point. Around the reboiler, L<sub>m</sub> − V<sub>m+1</sub> = B and H<sub>ΔB</sub> = h<sub>B</sub> − Q<sub>B</sub>/B, so Δ<sub>B</sub> = (x<sub>B</sub>, H<sub>ΔB</sub>) lies below the h curve.

Locating Δ<sub>B</sub> for a given feed. An overall balance F = D + B and F h<sub>F</sub> + Q<sub>B</sub> = D h<sub>D</sub> + B h<sub>B</sub> + Q<sub>C</sub> gives F h<sub>F</sub> = D H<sub>ΔD</sub> + B H<sub>ΔB</sub>, so Δ<sub>D</sub>, the feed point F = (z<sub>F</sub>, h<sub>F</sub>) and Δ<sub>B</sub> are collinear. Draw the line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through F and extend it to x = x<sub>B</sub>.

Stepping. From y<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>D</sub> on the H curve follow the tie line to x<sub>1</sub> on the h curve; draw the line from Δ<sub>D</sub> through x<sub>1</sub> to cut the H curve at y<sub>2</sub>; repeat. When the tie line crosses the line Δ<sub>D</sub>-F-Δ<sub>B</sub>, switch to Δ<sub>B</sub>. Count the tie lines; the last, at x ≤ x<sub>B</sub>, is the reboiler.

bank.q: Compare the McCabe-Thiele and Ponchon-Savarit methods. When does the constant molar overflow assumption fail, and why does this matter?
outline: McCabe-Thiele: y-x diagram only, needs constant molar overflow and constant latent heat
Ponchon-Savarit: uses enthalpy balance and enthalpy-concentration diagram, no constant molar overflow requirement
Constant molar overflow fails for wide boiling ranges, unequal latent heats, concentrated solutions, heat of mixing
Ponchon-Savarit also handles non-ideal equilibrium through the saturated curves
Cost: Ponchon-Savarit needs enthalpy data, more work per construction
answer: What each uses. McCabe-Thiele works on a y-x diagram with the equilibrium curve and straight operating lines from material balances alone. Ponchon-Savarit works on an enthalpy-composition diagram with the saturated H and h curves, tie lines and difference points, so it carries material and energy balances together.

McCabe-Thiele

answer: Constant molar overflow. McCabe-Thiele assumes that each mole of vapour condensing on a tray boils exactly one mole of liquid, so L and V are constant within each section. That needs (1) equal molar latent heats of the two components, (2) negligible heat of mixing, (3) negligible sensible-heat change from tray to tray, and (4) an adiabatic column.

When it fails. Unequal latent heats (ammonia-water, methanol-water), large heats of mixing (acid-water systems such as nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water), a wide boiling range so that sensible heat matters, and columns with heat losses or side heaters. On the enthalpy diagram these show up as H and h curves that slope differently or curve.

Why it matters. If L/V changes from tray to tray, the true operating line is curved. Using a straight line then misplaces every step: the stage count, the feed stage and the reboiler and condenser duties can all be wrong. In the chapter example with H = 50 − 10y and h = 20 − 4x, L/V fell from 0.663 to 0.653 over three trays instead of staying at 0.667, and the vapours drifted from the McCabe-Thiele values (0.7800 against 0.7764 after three trays). Over a long column such drift adds or removes stages.

The link. Ponchon-Savarit contains McCabe-Thiele as a limit. With horizontal H and h lines of constant gap λ, H<sub>ΔD</sub> = H<sub>V</sub> + Rλ and the lever rule gives L/V = Rλ/[(R + 1)λ] = R/(R + 1) on every tray: the straight McCabe-Thiele line returns.

Practical choice. McCabe-Thiele for nearly ideal pairs with similar latent heats (benzene-toluene) and for quick estimates and teaching. Ponchon-Savarit, or a rigorous simulation with enthalpy balances, for the non-CMO systems above and whenever the heat duties must be known with the stage count.

Closing check: for benzene (30.7 kJ/mol) and toluene (33.2 kJ/mol) the latent heats differ by about 8 %, small enough for McCabe-Thiele; for methanol (35.3) and water (40.7 kJ/mol) the difference is about 15 %, and the error grows with it.

bank.q: Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope. Explain why ordinary distillation cannot give pure ethanol and evaluate ways to break the azeotrope.
outline: At the azeotrope y = x, the equilibrium curve crosses the diagonal
The pinch point lies on the diagonal, so no finite number of stages crosses it
Options: change pressure (azeotrope composition moves), azeotropic distillation with an entrainer, extractive distillation with a heavy solvent, molecular sieve drying
Compare energy use, solvent recovery, capital cost
Choose based on scale and product purity needed
answer: The azeotrope. Ethanol-water shows a strong positive deviation from Raoult's law. At 1 atm the mixture of about 95.6 mass % ethanol (89.5 mol %) boils at 78.2 °C, below pure ethanol (78.4 °C) and pure water (100 °C). At that composition the vapour and liquid have the same composition: y = x and α = 1.

Why ordinary distillation stops there. On the y-x diagram the equilibrium curve lies above the diagonal for x below 0.895 and crosses it at the azeotrope. A column fed with dilute ethanol sends water to the bottoms, but the overhead can only approach 0.895: as the steps near the crossing they shrink to zero, because each stage needs y > x to make progress. Adding stages or reflux cannot move the distillate past it. Pure ethanol is not reachable from the water-rich side.

Mass balance illustration. From 100 kg of 50 mass % ethanol, all the ethanol taken overhead at the azeotrope gives D = 50/0.956 = 52.3 kg and water bottoms of 47.7 kg. The product is still 4.4 % water.

Option 1, pressure-swing distillation. The azeotrope composition shifts with pressure; for ethanol-water it becomes richer in ethanol at low pressure and disappears below roughly 10 kPa. Two columns at different pressures pass the azeotrope back and forth. No added chemical, but the shift for ethanol-water at practical pressures is small, so recycle and energy are large.

Option 2, azeotropic distillation. An entrainer (cyclohexane today, benzene in older plants) forms a lower-boiling ternary azeotrope that carries the water overhead. The overhead splits in a decanter into an entrainer layer (reflux) and a water layer (to a recovery column); dry ethanol leaves at the bottom. Proven, but it needs three columns and careful control, and benzene is toxic.

Option 3, extractive distillation. A high-boiling solvent (ethylene glycol) fed near the top lowers the volatility of water; ethanol goes overhead, water leaves with the solvent, and a second column recovers the glycol for recycle. Simpler and robust; the cost is solvent recovery energy and some solvent loss.

Option 4, molecular sieve adsorption. 3 Å zeolite beads adsorb water but not the larger ethanol molecule, in two beds alternating between adsorption and regeneration (pressure-swing adsorption), fed with azeotropic vapour. Low energy, no third chemical; the beds must be replaced after some years.

Verdict. For fuel-grade ethanol (99.5 % or more) most new plants distil to near the azeotrope and finish with molecular sieves, because the energy use is lowest. Extractive distillation suits large plants that already handle solvents; azeotropic distillation is now mostly found in older units.
Closing check: 95.6 mass % converts to (95.6/46.07)/(95.6/46.07 + 4.4/18.02) = 2.075/2.319 = 0.895 mole fraction, the crossing on the y-x diagram.

bank.q: Explain the economic trade-off in choosing the reflux ratio, and show why the optimum lies near a small multiple of the minimum reflux.
outline: Operating cost rises with R because reboiler and condenser duties rise roughly with R
Capital cost falls with R because fewer stages are needed
Total cost curve has a minimum, typically at R = 1.2 to 1.5 R<sub>min</sub>
Above the optimum, extra reflux is wasted; below it, stage count rises steeply
Practical limits: tray count, column height, pressure drop
answer: Two costs. The reflux ratio R = L/D fixes the vapour flow V = (R + 1)D, which sets the reboiler and condenser duties (energy cost) and the column diameter. It also fixes the stage count, which sets the column height. Annual cost = annualised capital (shell, trays, exchangers) + energy (steam and cooling water).
Energy cost rises with R. Reboiler duty ≈ V λ = (R + 1)Dλ, so steam and cooling water grow linearly with R + 1.

Capital cost falls, then rises. Near R<sub>min</sub> the stage count is very large, so the column is tall and expensive. As R rises the stages fall steeply at first, then level off toward N<sub>min</sub>. At high R the larger vapour flow needs a wider column and larger reboiler and condenser, so the capital cost climbs again.

answer.text: Stage count stepped off for α = 2.5, x<sub>F</sub> = 0.40 (saturated liquid), x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, x<sub>B</sub> = 0.05 (R<sub>min</sub> = 1.444, N<sub>min</sub> = 6.43):

answer: Reading the table. From 1.05 to 1.3 R<sub>min</sub> the energy rises by 14 % (2.52 to 2.88) while the stages fall by 30 % (20 to 14). From 2 to 3 R<sub>min</sub> the energy rises by 37 % for one stage saved. The first increments of reflux are cheap stages; later ones are expensive energy.

Total cost. A simple model with one cost unit per stage and six per unit of (R + 1) gives a total N + 6(R + 1) that is lowest near 1.34 R<sub>min</sub>, with a flat bottom between about 1.2 and 1.5 R<sub>min</sub>. Real cost data move the optimum within that range: high energy prices push it toward 1.1 to 1.2, cheap energy or expensive alloy columns toward 1.5 or more.

Why a small multiple. The stage count rises without bound as R → R<sub>min</sub>, so the optimum must be above R<sub>min</sub>; the energy keeps rising linearly, so the optimum cannot be far above. A steep left branch and a gently rising right branch put the minimum close to the left, at a small multiple of R<sub>min</sub>.

Other limits. Column height (a tall column needs a stronger foundation and more pressure drop), the turndown of the trays, and the margin needed for VLE uncertainty: designers rarely go below 1.1 R<sub>min</sub> because a small error in α can make the design unworkable.
Closing check: at R<sub>opt</sub> ≈ 1.3 R<sub>min</sub> = 1.878 the staircase gives 14 stages and Gilliland gives (6.43 + 0.505)/(1 − 0.505) = 14.0, so both routes agree on the design point.

The temperature at which the first bubble of vapour appears from a liquid mixture at a stated pressure.
The temperature at which the first drop of liquid condenses from a vapour mixture at a stated pressure.
A mixture obeying Raoult's law at every composition, with no heat of mixing.
A mixture whose equilibrium deviates from Raoult's law because of interactions or association; can show a maximum or minimum azeotrope.
The ratio of the vapour-liquid distribution coefficients of two components; values near 1 mean a hard separation.
An ideal contact stage in which the leaving vapour and liquid are in equilibrium.
Same as an equilibrium stage; the ideal plate or packing height that achieves one equilibrium contact.
Assumption that the liquid and vapour molar flows are the same in each section of the column, giving straight operating lines.
The part of the column below the feed, where the operating line lies below the diagonal and x decreases downwards.
The part of the column above the feed, enriched by reflux, where the operating line lies above the diagonal.
A condenser that turns all the overhead vapour into liquid; part returns as reflux and the rest leaves as distillate.
The overhead product withdrawn from the top of the column.
The liquid product withdrawn from the bottom of the column, richer in the less volatile component.
A heater at the base that boils part of the bottoms to supply vapour up the column; counted as one equilibrium stage.
A third component added in azeotropic distillation to carry the mixture past the azeotrope.
A high-boiling liquid that alters the relative volatility of the components without forming a new azeotrope.
An azeotrope that boils below both pure components (positive deviation from Raoult's law), such as ethanol-water at about 89.5 mol % ethanol.
The actual change in vapour composition across a real tray divided by the change an ideal tray would give.
Height of packed bed giving one theoretical stage; smaller HETP means more efficient packing.
A vertical shell with horizontal plates (sieve, valve or bubble-cap) on which vapour bubbles through liquid.
A column filled with rings, saddles or structured packing to give a large contact area for vapour and liquid.
The light and heavy components that define the required split in multicomponent distillation; the others are distributed.
The fixed point Δ on a Ponchon-Savarit diagram through which every operating line of one column section passes.
Heat to turn one mole of feed into saturated vapour divided by the molar latent heat; 1 for saturated liquid, 0 for saturated vapour.
